justification: Originality: the article's stated differentiator — find each pattern already compiled into the BCL (IComparer<T>, C# events/IObservable<T>, GZipStream/BufferedStream), name it, then hand-build a minimal version — is genuinely differentiated from the current landscape for 'design patterns c#'. Neither page does the BCL-first move this article is built around. This matches the task's premise and CONTENT_PLAN.md's row 5 angle exactly (patterns discovered in the BCL, not memorized from a catalogue). Sourcing: all 11 front-matter sources are real and I fetched all of them directly; all are cited inline (grep confirms every [[1]] through [[10]] index appears in the body, several multiple times). I checked every direct quotation against the live page text, character for character: List<T>.Sort's 'This implementation performs an unstable sort; that is, if two elements are equal, their order might not be preserved' (matches exactly, found in the full fetched page); 'Handling and raising events''s 'Events in .NET are based on the delegate model. The delegate model follows the observer design pattern' (matches exactly); IObservable<T>'s 'a generalized mechanism for push-based notification, also known as the observer design pattern' (matches exactly); GZipStream's 'may actually increase the size of the stream' (matches exactly, from the Remarks section on compressing already-compressed data); BufferedStream's 'can be composed around certain types of streams' and 'designed to prevent the buffer from slowing down input and output when the buffer is not needed' (both match exactly). Two claims that are paraphrase rather than quotation both check out too: the pitfall's assertion that Microsoft's own IObservable<T> sample snapshots the observer collection before notifying is true of the cited observer-design-pattern page's BaggageHandler example ('snapshot = [.. _observers];' before the foreach), and the GZipStream 'default is to dispose the stream it was given when it is itself disposed' claim matches the constructor page's Remarks verbatim in substance ('By default, GZipStream owns the underlying stream, so closing the stream parameter also closes the underlying stream'). Source [10] (the GoF book) is cited only for well-known, uncontroversial chapter-level facts (Strategy is behavioral, Decorator is structural) with no page number claimed, which is exactly what the editorial brief allows for a textbook that cannot be opened. No fabricated or altered quote anywhere. This is a pre-existing inaccuracy in a sibling article's crosslinks note, not in this article or its own crosslinks file, which already documents the conflation correctly ('the composition-over-inheritance note conflates the two interfaces, but the intent... is satisfied'). I did not edit the other file, per instructions; flagged below with owner integrator so it gets fixed at the source. The toolchain sentence ('compiled and run with dotnet run on .NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64') sits right before the first code block, not as the opening sentence, compliant with the binding rule. Structure varies meaningfully against both existing oop-design siblings: this article is organized as three pattern-named sections (Strategy/Observer/Decorator) with mostly statement headings, versus four-pillars-of-oop's question-heavy shape and composition-over-inheritance's single before/after refactoring narrative; CONTENT_PLAN.md §7.4 row 5 assigns this article shape W, distinct from both siblings' assigned shapes. One real finding keeps this off a higher score: the :::dotnet callout after the counting-stream example asserts 'Every Stream wrapper in this article disposes the stream it wraps by default when it is itself disposed' — true of BufferedStream and GZipStream (both verified against their docs), but not true of the article's own hand-built CountingStream, which does not override Dispose(bool) and therefore does not cascade-dispose its inner stream by default; the base Stream.Dispose(bool) implementation is a no-op. This is exactly the class of unscoped 'every' claim the pilot-round lessons call out, and it is untested by the article's own code (counting is never itself disposed in the example, so the claim is never exercised).
